Rituximab improves not only back stiffness but also “stiff eyes” in stiff
person syndrome: Implications for immune-mediated treatment
T

Keywords:
Stiff person plus
Slow saccade
Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD)
Video-based eye tracking system
Burst neurons
Omnipause neuron
Latch circuit

Objective: Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is usually characterized by truncal muscle rigidity and episodic painful
spasms, but it sometimes appears with ocular symptoms called “stiff eyes”. We recorded saccade movements in
an SPS patient manifesting with “stiff eyes” conditions with slow saccade velocity and evaluated the effect of
immunotherapy including rituximab on saccade parameters.
Methods: We repeatedly conducted saccade eye recordings using video-based eye tracking system on a 42-yearold male SPS patient with slow saccade. The velocity and onset latency of visual guided saccades (VGS) were
measured at each recording. Because VGS velocity is affected by saccade amplitude, estimated peak velocity
(Vmax) was also calculated by taking the relationship between the velocity and the amplitude of saccade into
account.
Results: The mean VGS velocity improved significantly after two courses of rituximab administration compared
with its lowest value. The estimated Vmax decreased as the clinical manifestations worsened, but it increased
after rituximab administration. Other neurological symptoms in this patient such as muscle rigidity and gait
instability also improved after the treatment.
Conclusion: Slow saccade in a “stiff eyes” patient improved after rituximab administration. Our study also indicated that the saccade eye recording is useful for evaluating the clinical condition of SPS when it is complicated with ocular symptoms.

1. Introduction
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a disabling chronic autoimmune
disorder of the central nervous system that is characterized by truncal
muscle rigidity, episodic and often painful muscle spasms, and high
titers of antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) [1–3].
Several clinical variants of SPS have previously been described as “stiff
person plus” [4], which is subcategorized into several entities: “stiff
limb syndrome”, which manifests as stiffness that is mainly found in the
limbs and sparing the trunk [4, 5]; and “jerking stiff person syndrome”,
which is accompanied by myoclonus [4, 6]. Some previous reports also
focused on abnormalities of eye movements in SPS, called “stiff eyes”
[7]. Nystagmus [8–10], slow saccades [7, 9, 10], multi-component saccades [10] and impaired saccade initiation [7, 10] have been reported

as manifestations of abnormal eye movement in SPS and are considered
to be related to the disturbance of GABAergic inhibitory neurotransmission that is caused by anti-GAD antibody activity within the
brainstem [10]. Although there are few previous studies on SPS with
eye movement disorders, a recent study showed that as many as 23% of
SPS patients manifested some ocular symptoms in a large cohort in the
United States [3].
Treatment of SPS includes GABA-enhancing drugs and intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIG) [11], but their efficacy is often partial and
transient [12]. Although several small case series have reported that
rituximab, which is monoclonal antibodies against CD20 cells that
causes B cell depletion, is effective for treating patients with SPS
[13–18], a recent double-blind placebo-controlled study in the United
States did not show statistically significant efficacy of rituximab in SPS

One major concern in previous rituximab case studies and clinical
trials for SPS is that the symptoms are mostly evaluated by the intensity
or distribution of stiffness, which is often affected by the patient's external environment or mental status. The placebo group and the rituximab group in the randomized-controlled trial showed a meaningful
improvement, which suggests that stiffness in SPS is strongly susceptible to placebo effects and may not be the best indicator for evaluating
treatment efficacy [12]. There is also a concern that stiffness is difficult
to assess quantitatively and that it is not sufficiently objective and lacks
reproducibility even when assessed by the same examiner. These factors
have necessitated novel approaches to measure the severity of SPS
symptoms to evaluate the true efficacy of treatments.
In a patient with SPS plus, we focused on ocular symptoms and took
this as a possible objective scale of the treatment with rituximab. We
measured several parameters of saccade eye movement using a videobased eye tracking system, which provides objective, quantitative, and
reproducible data (and may be less susceptible to the placebo effect).
We suggest that these methods enable precise evaluation of the disease
status and will facilitate further clinical trials of SPS accompanied by
ocular symptoms.
2. Methods
2. 1. Case presentation
Saccade recordings were conducted repeatedly in a patent with SPS
accompanied by eye movement disorders as part of the clinical assessment. The study was approved by the ethics committee of the
University of Tokyo Hospital and conducted after obtaining informed
consent from the patient.
The patient was a 42-year-old man with a history of hyperthyroidism and medial temporal lobe epilepsy resulting from left hippocampal sclerosis that had been surgically resected at age 31. When the
patient was 39 years old, he developed painful muscle spasms that affected his back muscles that showed a gradual increase in frequency
and intensity. He was diagnosed with SPS > 1 year after the onset based
on a high anti-GAD antibody level, as measured by radioimmunoassay,
and the results were 96, 000 IU/mL in the serum (reference

2. 2. Experimental setup
The experimental setup and data analysis procedures have been
described previously [19–22]. The patient's eye movements were recorded using a video-based eye tracking system that is now widely used
to record saccades (Eyelink II, SR Research Ltd., Ottawa, Canada).
The patient's saccade eye movements were recorded while he was
seated in front of a black, concave dome-shaped screen measuring 90cm in diameter that contained light-emitting diodes embedded in pinholes, which served as the fixation points and saccade targets. During
the recording, the patient's head was placed on a chin rest to restrict
head movements. The patient faced the center of the screen at a viewing
distance of about 66 cm and held a microswitch button that was connected to a microcomputer that allowed him to initiate and terminate a
trial by pressing the button with his thumb.
The room in which the recordings took place was kept dark except
for a small amount of ambient light around the examiner, so that the
unlit pinholes were not visible to the subject. The patient was asked to
sit in the dark for 20–30 min to allow for adaptation to the dark. There
was no change in ambient illumination throughout the experiment.

2. 4. Data analysis and statistical assessment
Two saccade parameters were determined off-line for each saccade,
as reported elsewhere [19–22]: velocity and onset latency. The onset of
an eye movement was defined as the time when velocity and acceleration exceeded predetermined values (28°/s and 90°/s2, respectively).
Eye movement was accepted as a saccade based on its velocity and
duration. After the onset, the velocity had to exceed 88°/s, and this
suprathreshold velocity had to be maintained for at least 10 ms. The
end of an eye movement was considered to have occurred when the
velocity decreased below 40°/s. The total duration of the movement
had to exceed 30 ms. Records contaminated by noise and those with
onset latency < 100 ms were excluded from the analysis. The mean
velocity and onset latency of 10°- and 20°-VGS were analyzed respectively using commercial software (SPSS, version 25; IBM Inc., Chicago,
IL, USA). The effect of the clinical time course on saccade parameters
was analyzed using a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA). Scheffe's

When assessing saccade velocity, we took into account the relationship between the amplitude and the peak velocity of saccades
[23], based on the methods of Bhidayasiri et al. [24], and the relationship can be described by the following equation:

Vmax = V0 × [1 − exp.(−AS/A 0)]
where V max is the maximal saccade velocity (peak velocity) and AS
is the saccade amplitude. Constants A0 and As were determined by
curve fitting using a commercial software (Origin Pro, version 8. 0 J;
Lightstone, Tokyo, Japan).

4. Discussion
Our study demonstrated improved velocity and onset latency of VGS
in a patient with SPS after rituximab administration. Although several
previous studies have reported eye movement abnormalities in SPS, it
was unknown whether these abnormalities are responsive to the immunomodulating treatments that are commonly used for SPS patients.
This is the first study that demonstrates the efficacy of rituximab on eye
movement abnormalities in SPS. Although past clinical trials did not
demonstrate the efficacy of rituximab in improving stiffness in SPS
patients, our results suggested that there is still a possibility that rituximab can modify symptoms other than stiffness, which awaits further confirmation in other cases.
A major issue in previous clinical studies in SPS has been the lack of
appropriate scales to evaluate the effects of treatment. Most previous
studies on the effect of rituximab for SPS used stiffness as the main
indicator of treatment. For example, Dalakas et al. used the stiffness
index that was determined by the distribution of stiffness as the primary
outcome, a hypersensitivity scale, and self-reported stiffness scores as
the secondary outcomes in their previous clinical trials [12]. However,
these scales are largely subjective and insensitive to the slight changes
in symptoms especially in less severe patients [12]. Some studies used
electromyographic recording of muscles with stiffness as an indicator of
clinical severity [13, 17], but the degree of stiffness may fluctuate easily
with emotional status and is subject to various other external factors
such as unexpected noises, tactile or visual stimuli [25], leading to its
low reproducibility as a clinical scale. The lack of reliable clinical scale
severity might have obscured the true effects of the drug for SPS. Some
studies used the anti-GAD antibody titers as a measure of improvement,
but the titer does not necessarily correlate with SPS clinical symptoms
[3, 26]. Thus, saccades can be precisely measured by the video-based
eye tracking system, as in this study, or using electrooculography,
which provides a more quantitative and reproducible measure in SPS
patients who present with ocular symptoms. Although saccade velocity
depends on saccade amplitude, the asymptoted peak velocity (Vmax)
can be estimated independent of saccade amplitude. Additionally, patients cannot choose to change the parameters of saccades, which
makes them resistant to placebo effects.
Although the precise pathophysiology that underlies eye movement
abnormalities in SPS remains unclear, the favorable outcome of rituximab in this patient allowed us to further speculate on the pathomechanisms. Physiologically, slow saccades are considered to arise
mainly as a result of the functional disruption of saccade burst neurons
within the brainstem saccade generator and/or the omnipause neuron
that inhibits the burst neurons. Additionally, a latch circuit is a recurrent pathway from the latch neuron, which is one component of the
saccadic burst generator and which projects back to further inhibit the
omnipause neurons (OPNs) for the duration of the saccade [27]. Sufficient suppression of the saccade burst neurons by OPNs is required for
a rapid increase in burst neuron firing subsequent to relieving this
suppression (post-inhibitory rebound) [27]. In SPS, anti-GAD antibodies may impair GABA transmission in CNS interneurons, and more

specifically, compromise the coordinated neuronal activities within the
brainstem oculomotor circuit, which connects the burst neurons, omnipause neurons, and latch circuit. A potential cause of slow saccades in
this patient may be the anti-GAD antibodies produced by CD20 cells
that act on this circuit, because the clinical findings including slow
saccades improved after rituximab administration; monoclonal

3. Results
Superimposed traces of both 10°- and 20°-VGS recorded in the patient are shown in Fig. 2 along with that of an age-matched normal
subject. At the early stage of the disorder, the saccade traces showed a
rapid rise at the onset of an eye movement and angular shaped trajectory. However, most saccade traces were composed of a series of
several small saccade steps before reaching the target, while eye
movements in normal subjects usually consisted of a single saccade. As
the clinical symptoms deteriorated, saccade traces changed into a “slow
eye movement” pattern that was characterized by curved trajectories
especially in the horizontal direction as shown in the traces after IVIG.
Then, the saccade traces seemed to improve at least to the level of the
early stage, and more specifically, it showed a rapid rise at the onset
and angular shaped trajectory, after the administration of rituximab.
The time courses of the velocity and the onset latency of VGS during
the follow-up period are shown in Fig. 3 with normal range of the agematched healthy population (data obtained in our laboratory from
thirty-seven healthy subjects between 36 and 45 years old). The velocity of 20°-VGS was slower than the lower limit of controls throughout
the follow up period, whereas that of 10°-VGS in the early stage was
within the normal limit. As the clinical symptoms deteriorated, the
mean velocity both of 10°- and 20°-VGS decreased to a nadir in the
second recording and then seemed to improve to a certain extent both
after IVIG and rituximab administration, although they were still slower
than the lower limit of normal range. The one-way ANOVA results indicated statistically significant changes in both 10°- and 20°-VGS velocity during the follow up periods (10°-VGS: F5, 93 = 8. 77, p < . 001;
20°-VGS: F5, 129 = 11. 92, p < . 001). The post-hoc analysis indicated a
significantly increased VGS velocity after rituximab administration
compared to its lowest value before IVIG, which was the time points II
and V (20°-VGS, p = . 008) and II and VI (10°-VGS, p = . 017; 20°-VGS,
p = . 008); VGS velocity also significantly decreased during the periods
before rituximab administration compared to that of the early stage,
and these time points were I and II (10°-VGS, p < . 001; 20°-VGS,
p < . 001), I and III (20°-VGS, p < . 001), and I and IV (10°-VGS,
p = . 012; 20°-VGS, p = . 003) (the Roman numerals correspond to those
described in the Methods). The mean onset latencies of 10°- and 20°VGS were mostly within the limit of age-matched normal controls
(mean plus and minus two standard deviations), whereas they seemed
to decrease moderately as the velocity improved. The one-way ANOVA

both 10°- and 20°-VGS during the follow up period (10°-VGS:
F5, 93 = 3. 02, p < . 001; 20°-VGS: F5, 129 = 4. 21, p < . 001). The posthoc analysis indicated that there was no significant difference among
each recording.
Although improvement of VGS velocity was described in Fig. 3, it is
not enough to simply assess changes in saccade velocity, because they
can be affected by saccade amplitudes. Thus, in Fig. 4, we plotted the
velocity of saccades against their amplitude, and curve fitting was
performed using the main sequence equation, as described in the
Methods, calculating estimated Vmax by taking into account the relationship between the saccade velocity and saccade amplitude [23].

Our study has several limitations. First, we conducted saccade recordings in only one patient without studying placebo-controlled subjects. We cannot exclude the possibility that the improvement of the eye
movement partially resulted from placebo effects. However, because
parameters of eye movement cannot be changed willingly and therefore
would be less susceptible to the placebo effect, we suggest that the
changes in saccade velocity represent genuine functional changes in the
brainstem oculomotor circuit. Similarly, it is also possible that the improvement in the saccade velocity reflected the natural course of the
disorder. Further clinical investigations are required to clarify the true
efficacy of rituximab on SPS. Second, it is not clear how the improvement of eye movement disorders relates to those of other commonly
observed symptoms in SPS such as stiffness and painful spasms. Thus,
we may not be able to directly extrapolate the favorable results of rituximab to other SPS patients without eye movement disorders.

Saccade eye movement in our case were also characteristic in that
they were composed of several small saccade steps, which was similar
to the findings described as “multi-component saccades” by Zivotofski
et al. [10]. This phenomenon was also observed in late-onset Tay-sachs
disease, and it has been considered to arise due to impaired latch circuit
function in brainstem [28]. On the other hand, downbeat nystagmus
was also observed in this case, which can be attributed to vestibulocerebellar dysfunction [10, 27] and rarely appears with brainstem lesions [27]. Because rituximab also improved downbeat nystagmus in
our study, GABAergic transmission in the interstitial nucleus of Cajal or
the pathways from Purkinje cells to medial vestibular nucleus, both of
which are related to vertical gaze holding [27], may have been involved
in this condition as well.
Another possible explanation for the ocular symptoms in this patient
is that autoantibodies other than anti-GAD antibodies may have played
a role in the patient's condition, because the changes in both the serum
and CSF levels of anti-GAD antibodies was slight and there was no
evidence that normal saccade is controlled by GABAergic

5. Conclusion
References

Slow saccades were observed in a patient with SPS, which improved
after rituximab administration. Although the precise mechanism for
this improvement remains unknown, it may be partially related to the
functional restoration of the brainstem oculomotor circuit, which involves the brainstem saccade generator (burst neurons), the omnipause
neuron, and/or the latch circuit. In patients with SPS who present with
stiff eyes syndrome, saccade abnormality, which is resistant to conscious control, may serve as a potential indicator for clinical severity
and it may be utilized in the assessment of clinical improvement associated with immunological treatment, affecting the neurotransmitters
within the above circuit. Our study suggested the possibility that further clinical trials may show the efficacy of rituximab for SPS if alternative scales for therapeutic effects such as saccades are used, at least
for the clinical presentation of “SPS plus”.

segments.text:
Objective: Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is usually characterized by truncal muscle rigidity and episodic painful
spasms, but it sometimes appears with ocular symptoms called “stiff eyes”. We recorded saccade movements in
an SPS patient manifesting with “stiff eyes” conditions with slow saccade velocity and evaluated the effect of
immunotherapy including rituximab on saccade parameters.
Methods: We repeatedly conducted saccade eye recordings using video-based eye tracking system on a 42-yearold male SPS patient with slow saccade. The velocity and onset latency of visual guided saccades (VGS) were
measured at each recording. Because VGS velocity is affected by saccade amplitude, estimated peak velocity
(Vmax) was also calculated by taking the relationship between the velocity and the amplitude of saccade into
account.
Results: The mean VGS velocity improved significantly after two courses of rituximab administration compared
with its lowest value. The estimated Vmax decreased as the clinical manifestations worsened, but it increased
after rituximab administration. Other neurological symptoms in this patient such as muscle rigidity and gait
instability also improved after the treatment.
Conclusion: Slow saccade in a “stiff eyes” patient improved after rituximab administration. Our study also indicated that the saccade eye recording is useful for evaluating the clinical condition of SPS when it is complicated with ocular symptoms.

3. Results
Superimposed traces of both 10°- and 20°-VGS recorded in the patient are shown in Fig. 2 along with that of an age-matched normal
subject. At the early stage of the disorder, the saccade traces showed a
rapid rise at the onset of an eye movement and angular shaped trajectory. However, most saccade traces were composed of a series of
several small saccade steps before reaching the target, while eye
movements in normal subjects usually consisted of a single saccade. As
the clinical symptoms deteriorated, saccade traces changed into a “slow
eye movement” pattern that was characterized by curved trajectories
especially in the horizontal direction as shown in the traces after IVIG.
Then, the saccade traces seemed to improve at least to the level of the
early stage, and more specifically, it showed a rapid rise at the onset
and angular shaped trajectory, after the administration of rituximab.
The time courses of the velocity and the onset latency of VGS during
the follow-up period are shown in Fig. 3 with normal range of the agematched healthy population (data obtained in our laboratory from
thirty-seven healthy subjects between 36 and 45 years old). The velocity of 20°-VGS was slower than the lower limit of controls throughout
the follow up period, whereas that of 10°-VGS in the early stage was
within the normal limit. As the clinical symptoms deteriorated, the
mean velocity both of 10°- and 20°-VGS decreased to a nadir in the
second recording and then seemed to improve to a certain extent both
after IVIG and rituximab administration, although they were still slower
than the lower limit of normal range. The one-way ANOVA results indicated statistically significant changes in both 10°- and 20°-VGS velocity during the follow up periods (10°-VGS: F5, 93 = 8. 77, p < . 001;
20°-VGS: F5, 129 = 11. 92, p < . 001). The post-hoc analysis indicated a
significantly increased VGS velocity after rituximab administration
compared to its lowest value before IVIG, which was the time points II
and V (20°-VGS, p = . 008) and II and VI (10°-VGS, p = . 017; 20°-VGS,
p = . 008); VGS velocity also significantly decreased during the periods
before rituximab administration compared to that of the early stage,
and these time points were I and II (10°-VGS, p < . 001; 20°-VGS,
p < . 001), I and III (20°-VGS, p < . 001), and I and IV (10°-VGS,
p = . 012; 20°-VGS, p = . 003) (the Roman numerals correspond to those
described in the Methods). The mean onset latencies of 10°- and 20°VGS were mostly within the limit of age-matched normal controls
(mean plus and minus two standard deviations), whereas they seemed
to decrease moderately as the velocity improved. The one-way ANOVA
results indicated statistically significant changes in onset late cues of
both 10°- and 20°-VGS during the follow up period (10°-VGS:
F5, 93 = 3. 02, p < . 001; 20°-VGS: F5, 129 = 4. 21, p < . 001). The posthoc analysis indicated that there was no significant difference among
each recording.
Although improvement of VGS velocity was described in Fig. 3, it is
not enough to simply assess changes in saccade velocity, because they
can be affected by saccade amplitudes. Thus, in Fig. 4, we plotted the
velocity of saccades against their amplitude, and curve fitting was
performed using the main sequence equation, as described in the
Methods, calculating estimated Vmax by taking into account the relationship between the saccade velocity and saccade amplitude [23].

segments.text:
Slow saccades were observed in a patient with SPS, which improved
after rituximab administration. Although the precise mechanism for
this improvement remains unknown, it may be partially related to the
functional restoration of the brainstem oculomotor circuit, which involves the brainstem saccade generator (burst neurons), the omnipause
neuron, and/or the latch circuit. In patients with SPS who present with
stiff eyes syndrome, saccade abnormality, which is resistant to conscious control, may serve as a potential indicator for clinical severity
and it may be utilized in the assessment of clinical improvement associated with immunological treatment, affecting the neurotransmitters
within the above circuit. Our study suggested the possibility that further clinical trials may show the efficacy of rituximab for SPS if alternative scales for therapeutic effects such as saccades are used, at least
for the clinical presentation of “SPS plus”.
